extracted.intended_audience: proofreaders, copyholders, compositors, editors, and authors working for (or with) an academic press/typographical shop
extracted.subtask_description: A press-oriented manual of typographical and editorial rules (capitalization, italics, quotations, punctuation, divisions, footnotes, tabular work, technical terms, specimen type usage) intended to standardize composition and production for publications of the University of Chicago Press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface: Rules as flexible guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and regulations are meant for the average case and must be applied with elasticity; exceptions will constantly occur and room is left for individual initiative and discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules point the way rather than serve as absolute law; deviations are legitimate when the subject-matter, emphasis, author's preference, or typographical contingency suggests it. Generally defer to the expressed wishes of the author where questions of mere preference (not taste or logic) arise. The Manual is practical rather than exhaustive or inflexibly consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Proper nouns and adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: George, America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French. See also rule 46 for derived adjectives and verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Generic terms forming part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms when they form an organic part of geographical names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Atlantic Ocean, Dead Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi River, Pike's Peak, Mount of Olives. Do not capitalize when the term is merely descriptive and not an organic part: the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Adjectives and nouns distinguishing definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or together to denote definite regions or parts of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole, the Far East, Orient. Do not, as a rule, capitalize adjectives derived from such names used in general senses: oriental customs, southern states, a southerner (exceptions noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Generic terms for political divisions (when part of name)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic political-division terms when (i) they directly follow the proper name as an organic part, (ii) used with 'of' in direct connection indicating minor administrative subdivisions in the U.S., (iii) used singly as accepted designation, or (iv) used as a fanciful/popular appellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Holy Roman Empire, French Republic, Northwest Territory, Department of the Lakes, the Union, the Republic, Celestial Empire. Do not capitalize such terms when standing alone or when used with 'of' preceding the specific name (the empire, kingdom of Belgium, state of Illinois).

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize numbered political divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings and similar place names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block, Lakeside Building, White House. Do not capitalize general designations (courthouse, post-office, library) except in connection with the place name.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Names of political parties, religious denominations, schools and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of parties, denominations, philosophical/literary/artistic schools and their adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Republican, Christian, Evangelical Lutheran, Catholic, Romantic movement, Symbolic school of painters. Do not capitalize such words (or their derivatives) when used in a general or pervasive sense: republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea, catholicity of mind, epicurean tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuitism.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize official titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Union League Club, Young People's Society of Christian Endeavor, Smithsonian Institution, The Macmillan Company, Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad. Do not capitalize generic terms used as class names or when standing alone unless needed to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Names of legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies when specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of governmental bodies and departments and their branches when specifically applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior, Chicago City Council. Do not capitalize general or paraphrastic references: the national assembly, the council, the department.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Ordinals designating dynasties, sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, and similar connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress, the Second Illinois Regiment Band.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Appellations for historical epochs and geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted names for historical epochs, literary/language periods, and geological ages and strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stone Age, Middle Ages, Renaissance, Old English, Pleistocene, Silurian.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of important historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thirty Years' War, Civil War, War of 1812, Battle of Gettysburg, Louisiana Purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Political alliances and historically significant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and terms from secular or ecclesiastical history that have acquired special significance as designations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, the Roundheads.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions, and similar gatherings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Council of Nicaea, Parliament of Religions, Chicago World's Fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize formal titles of treaties, acts, laws, and juridical documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Treaty of Verdun, Art. V of the Peace of Prague, Declaration of Independence, Magna Charta. Use 'the Constitution' as capitalized when referring to the U.S. Constitution standing alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of creeds and confessions of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Apostles' Creed, Augsburg Confession, Thirty-nine Articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Civic and ecclesiastical feast-days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of civic and ecclesiastical feast-days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fourth of July (the Fourth), Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Easter, Passover. Note: 'sabbath' (as day of rest) is lowercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Titles preceding names and abbreviated academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize civil and military titles preceding the name, and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name; capitalize titles of nobility and purely honorary titles when referring to specific persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D.; 'the President' (when referring to U.S. President) and similar usages. Do not capitalize titles of occupants of offices when following the name (McKinley, president of the United States) or when standing alone in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Abbreviated titles without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Set abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S. without spaces between letters and capitalize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When spelled out (doctor of philosophy, fellow of the Royal Geographical Society) do not capitalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Names/designations for the Deity and pronouns referring to Deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or any member of the Christian Trinity, and pronouns referring to the Deity when not immediately preceded or followed by a distinctive name and when the reference is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Almighty, Providence, Father, Son, Holy Ghost, Savior, Messiah. Do not capitalize derivatives like 'God's fatherhood' in ordinary usage; also example 'When God had worked six days, he rested on the seventh.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Personified abstract terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar terms and abstract ideas when personified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Nature wields her scepter mercilessly;'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. 'Father' for church father; 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' used for church father and 'Reformers' used of Reformation leaders when ambiguity would otherwise result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Fathers, the early Fathers, the Reformers (but 'the church reformers of the fifteenth century' lowercase).

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. 'Church' in cited titles of nationally organized bodies or in building names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the word 'Church' in properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies and when part of a building's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Church of Rome, Church of England, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church. Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone or when the name is not fully quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize commonly accepted names for the Bible and other sacred books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (Holy, Sacred) Scriptures, Holy Writ, Word of God, Book of Books, Koran, Vedas. Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns ('biblical', 'scriptural').

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Versions of the English Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of versions of the English Bible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Authorized Version (A. V.), Revised Version (R. V.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. Books and divisions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of books and divisions of the Bible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Old Testament, Pentateuch, Exodus, Second Kings, Psalms, Gospel of Luke. Do not capitalize 'book', 'gospel', 'epistle', or 'psalm' in generic references: the five books of Moses, the first forty psalms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of biblical parables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Parables of the Prodigal Son and the Lost Coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Miscellaneous biblical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize specific important biblical terms and titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve (apostles), the Psalmist.

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. First word of a sentence and first word in poetry lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and, in English poetry, the first word of each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Greek and Latin poetry capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. First word after a colon (when it introduces an independent sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when it introduces a complete passage or sentence that would stand independently or when the colon has the force of 'as follows' or similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In conclusion I wish to say: It will be seen from the above that ...' Do not capitalize if the quotation is immediately connected with what precedes or if the colon introduces a dependent phrase or note of comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. First word in sections of enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, capitalize the first word in sections of enumeration if any individual item contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolons, colons, or periods, unless all are dependent upon the same term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided demonstrating when enumeration clauses begin with capitals vs. when they do not. See also rule 125.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Nouns followed by numerals indicating sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by numerals indicating order in a sequence, particularly with capital Roman numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Room 16, Ps. 20, Grade IV, Art. II, Act I; Vol. I, No. 2 (for journals). Do not capitalize minor subdivisions like sec. 4, scene i, chap. 2(ii). See rule 100 for abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. First word of a cited speech in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse whether preceded by a colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'On leaving he remarked: 'Never shall I forget this day;'' and similar constructions (also applies without quotation marks in running text).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. First words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions (these are preceded by a comma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whereas, It has pleased God ...; therefore be it Resolved, That ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. The exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O Lord!' 'Oh, that I were home again!'

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Principal words in English titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and their divisions, subjects of lectures, certain heads, and box-heads in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Men Who Made the Nation; The American College — Its Past and Present. Note: the definite article 'the' is not treated as part of newspaper/magazine titles unless necessary (the Forum, the Chicago Tribune). Foreign-title capitalization rules vary by language (Latin, French, German, etc.). Botanical Gazette exception noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS/MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Codex Bezae, Vatican Palimpsest, Oxyrhynchus Logia.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. Nouns in hyphenated compounds in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Twentieth-Century Progress', 'The Economy of High-Speed Trains.' Do not capitalize hyphen components when other than nouns (e.g., 'Fifty-first Street', 'Lives of Well-known Authors').

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. Scientific Latin names for higher taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera in zoological/botanical/technical matter; names of species are lower-case (except when proper names in nominative/genitive or proper adjectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vertebrata, Reptilia, Cruciferae, Salix; species names generally set in italics (see rule 61).

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Names of solar-system bodies in astronomical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of bodies of our solar system in astronomical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sun, Moon, Earth, the Milky Way.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. University of Chicago internal divisions and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work dealing with its administration or curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the School of Education (the School), the Department of Anthropology (but 'the department' lowercase), the Board of Trustees, Professor of Physics. The rule is specific to the University context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Use capitals and small capitals for date and salutatory lines in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals and small capitals for the names of town and state in the dateline, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and for signature/residence lines at the end of letters or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1906' (set to the right, smaller type); 'My dear Mr. Smith:' (flush, followed by colon). Styles for multi-line addresses are specified (first line caps & small caps, second line caps & lower-case centered).

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Use of 'Whereas' and 'Note' and 'Section' in formal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Whereas' in resolutions; capitalize 'Note' in notes (not footnotes) followed by a period and dash; capitalize 'Section' introducing paragraphs in constitutions, by-laws, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Note. — It should be noticed that ...' 'Section i. This association shall be styled ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Set in small capitals: A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. (ante and post meridiem) and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals with a thin space between letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Use small initial letter for words once proper names now common
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally for verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia (proper), bohemian, philistine, titanic (adjectives), boycott, anglicize, macadamized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Lowercase minor subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references such as chapter, section, page, verse, line, note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references: See rules 33, 100, and 218 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Italic side-heads: lowercase after first word
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set the remainder in lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations referenced (156 and 261).

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. First word of a quotation connected with preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for the first word of a quotation which is immediately connected with what precedes, even if the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 118 for illustration and exceptions; compare rule 31.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or importance is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case;' 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life ...' Use italics sparingly for rhetorical emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Italics for foreign words/phrases not anglicized
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign words and phrases inserted into English text that are not incorporated into English, and single sentences/brief passages in another language not long enough to set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'coup d'état', 'par excellence', many French/Latin phrases. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of institutions/places that have become standard in roman usage (e.g., Pére Lagrange, Reichstag, Champs Elysées). A list of common foreign words that are italicized appears in the Manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Italics for titles of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of books, plays, long poems printed separately, pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals (including journals' names appearing in their own pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Chicago Tribune, Report of the United States Commissioner of Education. Note: Books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts should be set in roman (see rules 27 and 38).

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Italics for certain bibliographic terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize bibliographical/Latin terms used in literary references: ibid., idem, loc. cit., op. cit., ad loc., s. v., supra, infra, passim, vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize abbreviations like cf., i.e., e.g. (set with a thin space).

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Italics for address lines in speeches and primary address lines in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize/address-format primary address lines in speeches, reports, and letters (e.g., 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:' and 'Mr. John Smith, 121 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set these flush in a separate line with nouns capitalized (see rule 43 for caps & small caps usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Italics in signatures for position/title after name
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize position or title added after the name in signatures; placement depends on length relative to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one word, run into same line with name; if longer, center or indent according to detailed placement rules. Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' and 'Carter H. Harrison \n Mayor of Chicago'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italics for subsection markers (a), b), c) and fractional verse/page letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize subsection markers a), b), c), etc., used to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph; double parentheses if 'run in'); also a, b, c affixed to numerals to denote fractional parts of verses/pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:31a (with a hair-space).

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Italics for letters designating unknown quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize letters used to designate unknown quantities, lines, and powers in algebraic and geometrical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac + bc = (a + b)c; the lines ad and AD; the wth power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italics for letters in legends referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize letters in legends or in the text that refer to corresponding letters in illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).' Use italics for single-letter references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italics for references to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize references to particular letters as objects of discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the letter u, a small v.

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italics for s. and d. (shillings and pence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize s. and d. following numerals to indicate shillings and pence (with a hair-space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 3s. 6d.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italics for scientific species names and astronomical stars
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize scientific (Latin) names of species in zoological/botanical matter and names of stars or constellations in astronomical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina; Saturn, Cassiopeia.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italics for 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the word 'Resolved' when used in resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 35 for context (resolutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italics for 'Continued' after headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize 'Continued' after headlines as a rule, and include '[To be continued]' at the end of articles when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline formatting: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY — Continued. At article end: [To be continued].

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Quotation marks for in-text author citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (roman-quote) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 75 for longer quotations and reduced-type treatment; inline citations remain in roman type within quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Put in quotation marks quotations from different authors following each other uninterrupted by any intervening original matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quoting multiple authors back-to-back, each quotation is enclosed appropriately to indicate attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Quotation marks for a word or phrase accompanied by its definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks when a word or phrase is accompanied by its definition within the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-fold' means a page-number at the bottom of the page; Such a piece of metal is called a 'slug.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironic words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironic, or attention-directed words or phrases in the text, whether or not accompanied by words like 'so-called'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; a self-styled 'connoisseur.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Quotation marks for English translations of foreign words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Put in quotation marks the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage used in translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen, Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. Quotation marks to mark the particular word(s) being discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word or words to which attention is directed in discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; use quotation marks when analyzing or discussing word-usage.
